A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {M, d}$ be a [[Definition:Metric Space|metric space]].
Then $x_n \to x$ {{iff}} $\map d {x_n, x} \to 0$, a sequence is [[Definition:Cauchy Sequence (Metric Space)|Cauchy]] {{iff}} $\map d {x_m, x_n} \to 0$, and $f$ is [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Metric Spaces)|continuous]] {{iff}} the $\epsilon$-$\delta$ condition holds with $d$ in place of $\size {x - y}$.

B_source.statement: On $\R$, $x_n \to x$ {{iff}} $\size {x_n - x} \to 0$, and continuity and Cauchyness are defined using $\size {x - y}$.

substitutions.the ordering of the reals: no ordering, only the triangle inequality
substitutions.completeness of R: completeness as an extra hypothesis rather than a theorem

derived.the epsilon-delta definitions: the same definitions with d in place of absolute value

validity_conditions: only the metric axioms may be used, so arguments relying on the order structure of R do not transfer
completeness must be assumed rather than derived, since general metric spaces are not complete
results using local compactness, such as Bolzano-Weierstrass, require additional hypotheses
proof_plan: The real-line proofs use only the following properties of $\size {x - y}$: non-negativity, symmetry, the [[Triangle Inequality]], and $\size {x - y} = 0 \iff x = y$.
Adopt exactly these as the [[Definition:Metric Space Axioms|metric space axioms]] for $d$.

Restate convergence, Cauchyness and continuity with $d$.
Proofs such as [[Limit of Sequence is Unique]] and [[Convergent Sequence is Cauchy Sequence]] go through verbatim.
Arguments using the order of $\R$, such as the [[Monotone Convergence Theorem (Real Analysis)|Monotone Convergence Theorem]], or the completeness of $\R$, do not transfer.

Reintroduce [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|completeness]] or [[Definition:Compact Metric Space|compactness]] as explicit hypotheses where these arguments are needed.
{{qed}}
